children: By Roshan Fernandez
Hundreds of colleges are sending students letters of admission-without even requiring an application.

Schools are increasingly agreeing to admit students based on a handful of criteria, like high school transcripts. Known as "direct admissions," this expedited process is free and omits required essays, questions about extracurriculars and mandated standardized tests.

In turn, the colleges-which are seeking ways to attract more students amid broader financial headwinds-gain exposure to prospects who may never have heard of them otherwise. They then woo the young people into enrolling.
Proponents call the approach a solution for both sides.

"Instead of a student applying to the institution, the institution applies to them," said Angel Perez, chief executive of the National Association for College Admission Counseling. "It's a way for students not to have to jump through hoops in order to get into college."

Direct admission has ballooned in popularity, particularly among less-selective private schools vying for a shrinking pool of college-goers. On the Common App, the number of participating institutions has more than tripled since 2023-24, representing about a fifth of the app's partners, said Chief Executive Jenny Rickard. More than a dozen states now have direct-admissions initiatives.

"We can no longer take a posture that expects our students to come to us," said Karlyn Crowley, president of Kalamazoo College in Michigan, which added direct admissions this year. "We're at a new moment."

Colleges across America are reckoning with the demographic cliff as the pipeline of 18-year-olds dwindles. Lesser-known campuses sit at the forefront of these enrollment challenges, though cracks are spreading throughout. And since most colleges admit more than half of applicants-the acceptance rate in the U.S. topped 70% among four-year, not-for-profit schools in a 2023 NACAC report-supporters say direct admissions is a no-brainer.

"This is the attempt of a lot of institutions, including ourselves, to get in front of more students and increase the top of that enrollment funnel," said Andy Otto, vice president of enrollment management at Missouri Western State University.

The process aims to be straightforward: students interested in direct admissions fill out a form-not a full application-on various sites that essentially act as matchmakers. The students, or their high schools, also submit their transcripts. From there, the offers roll in automatically. (As with the traditional pathway, though, colleges can yank acceptances if a teen's grades tank in their senior year.)

Eden Johnson, a high-school senior, recently got a direct-admission offer to Fort Valley State University in Georgia as part of a summer program she did there. "I thought getting into college would be scarier," she said, "but it just felt exciting."
Johnson, who plans to study biology, still compiled a list of around 20 colleges, and will complete traditional applications for many.
Though Fort Valley State is a backup option for her, the acceptance helped negate some self-doubt. "It just felt good to be wanted somewhere," she said.
That shift, highlighting acceptances instead of rejections, is an appeal for many young people.

"It's kind of like the dating world," said Jessica Wiggins, vice president of enrollment management at Jacksonville State University, which added direct admissions as part of a statewide initiative launched last year. It is easier to focus on the people who are interested in you, she said.

For that northeast Alabama school, the strategy appears to be helping. Jacksonville State typically drew candidates from nearby counties, but in the last cycle it also attracted applicants in droves from the southern and western parts of the state.

It received around 2,000 direct-admit submissions, and enrolled about 150 to 200 students, a lower yield rate than for standard admission but still a net positive. Rickard, from the Common App, said yield usually runs lower for direct admissions because schools have less time to court prospects, many of whom know little about the institution beforehand.

Chandra Scott, executive director of Alabama Possible, which oversees the state's direct-admission program, likens the sign-up form for students to a social-media profile: something they can do "in their sleep."

Not everyone is sold. Critics say direct admission muddies an already-confusing process with countless invitations. Some schools are unclear about financial commitments accompanying offers. "There's a big difference between getting in and being able to afford to go," said Beth Kraemer, founder of In College Consulting.
To combat this, Alabama made sure participating institutions deliver price information within initial offer letters.

On another site, Niche, where more than 160 institutions will offer direct admissions this cycle, students receive immediate merit aid offers based on their grades, and are still eligible to apply for additional scholarships and financial aid. The average user gets over $17,000 in scholarships a year, said Chief Executive Luke Skurman.
Niche said the initiative is attracting a larger share of first-generation students and those of color than traditional admissions.
Overall, Niche says students receive an average of eight direct admissions offers. For schools, convincing the prospects to enroll can be the hardest part.

"Our best pitch is to put the money on the table," said Ryan Fewins-Bliss, executive director of Michigan College Access Network, which launched the state's direct-admissions program last month. That cost transparency allows applicants to compare offers.
